source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

In the bustling line, a humdrum melody played—metal trays clinking, luggage conveyor belts churning. Each traveler divested their belongings, each item laid out in neat rows under scanners that glowed with cold, clinical certainty.

At the end of the queue, an officer beckoned, his hand gesturing to the first in line, a young woman whose cheeks flushed beneath the scrutiny of metal detectors humming softly above her. The woman’s documents were scrutinized; the officer then stepped forward, hands reaching for a brief pat-down, eyes steady and unyielding.

Ahead, a sign read “All Passengers Proceed,” its words etched with the impersonal courtesy of authority. Another queue formed around the next checkpoint as the scanners continued their vigilant watch.

The woman’s bag was placed on a tray; she watched it as it slid smoothly through the scanner. The machine whirred, images projected onto a screen above. Meanwhile, another traveler stood nervously by, awaiting their turn, documents in hand and a slight tremor in their grip.

As the officer moved to the next person, the woman’s bag was marked with an icon—proceeding to security checks. She followed suit, each step a dance of compliance under the watchful eye of metal detectors.

At another checkpoint, two officers flagged down a man, his documents held out for inspection. The man’s belongings were divested into trays; a pat-down commenced as another officer stepped in. His bag was scanned, icon appearing on the screen—proceed to next station.

The register of control was clear and unwavering: instructions posted at every turn, each step monitored meticulously by those vested with authority. Signage directed travelers through the labyrinth of checkpoints, each part a cog in the machine of security.

In the heart of the line, another traveler’s bag displayed a different icon—suspect item detected. The officer stepped forward, hands reaching for a more thorough pat-down as the scanner whirred to life above.

At the bustling checkpoint, the queue stretched like an uncoiling serpent, and the barriers loomed, a daunting gate of metal. Each traveler divested themselves into trays, their items laid out in neat piles, awaiting inspection by scanners and metal detectors.

A pair was singled out from the line; the officer's stern gaze cut through the cacophony. "Please, hand over your documents," he said, his voice a monotone of authority. The passenger hesitated, then did as instructed.

Meanwhile, the body-search gesture began in earnest, a ritual of control conducted by the very machine that scanned their belongings. A second officer approached the traveler, fingers gliding across their skin, the familiar sensation of the impersonal courtesy of authority.

"Please move through the scanner," he said, and she complied, stepping into the narrow channel where her image was scrutinized. The instructions on the screen above were clear: follow the signs to proceed. She moved forward with measured steps, guided by unseen hands.

As she emerged from the checkpoint, the officer's voice echoed once more, "Have a safe journey," before turning back to face the next pair in line. The queue continued its slow progress, each traveler experiencing the register of control as if it were an unwritten contract.

Her documents returned, the traveler gathered her belongings and moved forward, stepping over the threshold where the barriers separated two realities: one of uncertainty and scrutiny, the other of freedom. Her eyes met those of another traveler, both sharing a momentary recognition, a silent acknowledgment of the journey that lay ahead.
